claims.statement: An adaptation claim is interpretable only against a frozen behavior/configuration/evaluation baseline.
Target gains, retained capabilities, controls, resource budgets, and rejection criteria should precede training.
Upstream defects must be ruled out before attributing a failure to model weights.
Tokenizer, template, architecture, position/context mechanism, precision, and checkpoint are separate model-system surfaces.
Token fragmentation can change effective sequence length and multilingual/domain representation.
Architecture inspection identifies plausible intervention surfaces but cannot predict task improvement without experiments.
Prompt/context repair, SFT, PEFT, preference optimization, distillation, continued pretraining, and model replacement target different failure hypotheses.
Weight access, data quality, compute, reversibility, runtime, and control requirements constrain available interventions.
At least one plausible intervention should be rejected using predicted evidence or boundary constraints before experimentation expands.
A data recipe identifies sources, rights/permissions, example schema, inclusion/exclusion, quality, mixture, transformations, reviewers, versions, and limitations.
Synthetic instruction data can scale examples but may reproduce generator errors and biases.
Multilingual mixtures need explicit language/task balance and separate evaluation.
Deduplication can reduce memorization and evaluation contamination but thresholds and scope create tradeoffs.
Train, development, evaluation, retention, and control sets need explicit separation and identity.
Filtering and normalization choices alter the learned distribution and must be recorded as data decisions.
Instruction examples must map to target behavior clauses, errors, and segments rather than convenience prompts.
Chat template and loss masking determine which tokens contribute to SFT learning.
Negative, abstention, and boundary cases are needed when the contract requires non-answer behavior.
